category: Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox > Probability Distributions & Hypothesis Testing
description: Creating and fitting probability distribution objects, evaluating densities and quantiles, generating random data, descriptive statistics, and the classical parametric and nonparametric hypothesis tests.

tools.name: makedist
tools.description: Create a probability distribution object with parameters you specify, rather than fitting them to data. The returned object works with pdf, cdf, icdf, random, mean, var and truncate. Use it to define a known theoretical distribution for simulation or comparison.
tools.usage:
pd = makedist(distname)
pd = makedist(distname, Name, Value)
list = makedist

tools.name: fitdist
tools.description: Fit a probability distribution to sample data by maximum likelihood and return a distribution object. It supports censoring, frequency weights and fitting separate distributions per group. Use it to characterize empirical data with a parametric model.
tools.usage:
pd = fitdist(x, distname)
pd = fitdist(x, distname, Name, Value)
[pdca, gn, gl] = fitdist(x, distname, 'By', groupvar)

parameters.name: 'By'
parameters.description: Grouping variable so one distribution is fitted per group.

parameters.name: 'Frequency'
parameters.description: Integer counts giving the number of observations at each x value.

tools.notes: Compare candidate families with negloglik, and check the fit with probplot or a KS test.

tools.name: pdf
tools.description: Evaluate a probability density (or mass) function, either from a distribution object or from a distribution name with explicit parameters. It is the generic front end to the family of specific functions such as normpdf and gampdf. Use it to plot densities and compute likelihoods.
tools.usage:
y = pdf(pd, x)
y = pdf(name, x, A, B, C, D)

parameters.name: pd
parameters.description: A probability distribution object from makedist or fitdist.

parameters.name: A, B, ...
parameters.description: Distribution parameters when using the name form.

tools.name: cdf
tools.description: Evaluate a cumulative distribution function from a distribution object or by name with parameters. It gives the probability that a random variable is less than or equal to each value in x. Use it for p-values, tail probabilities and probability plots.
tools.usage:
p = cdf(pd, x)
p = cdf(name, x, A, B, C, D)
p = cdf(___, 'upper')

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Values at which to evaluate the CDF.

parameters.name: 'upper'
parameters.description: Return the complementary (upper tail) probability, computed accurately for small values.

tools.name: icdf
tools.description: Evaluate the inverse cumulative distribution function (quantile function) of a distribution at given probabilities. It answers questions such as 'what value is exceeded 5% of the time'. Use it to compute critical values, confidence bounds and to generate samples by inverse transform.
tools.usage:
x = icdf(pd, p)
x = icdf(name, p, A, B, C, D)

tools.name: random
tools.description: Generate random numbers from a probability distribution object or a named distribution with parameters. It is the generic sampler that covers every distribution supported by the toolbox. Combine with rng for reproducible simulations.
tools.usage:
r = random(pd)
r = random(pd, m, n)
r = random(name, A, B, m, n)

parameters.name: A, B, ...
parameters.description: Distribution parameters for the name form.

tools.name: normrnd
tools.description: Generate normally distributed random numbers with specified mean and standard deviation. Parameters can be arrays, in which case each output element uses the corresponding parameters. It is the most direct way to simulate Gaussian data with a non-unit scale.
tools.usage:
r = normrnd(mu, sigma)
r = normrnd(mu, sigma, sz1, ..., szN)
r = normrnd(mu, sigma, sz)

parameters.name: sigma
parameters.description: Standard deviation, scalar or array, must be nonnegative.

tools.notes: mu + sigma*randn(m,n) is equivalent and does not require the toolbox.

tools.name: mvnrnd
tools.description: Generate random vectors from a multivariate normal distribution with a given mean vector and covariance matrix. The covariance must be symmetric positive semi-definite. Use it to simulate correlated measurements and to build synthetic classification data.
tools.usage:
R = mvnrnd(mu, Sigma)
R = mvnrnd(mu, Sigma, n)

parameters.name: mu
parameters.description: 1-by-d mean vector, or n-by-d for per-observation means.

parameters.name: Sigma
parameters.description: d-by-d covariance matrix (or d-by-d-by-n for per-observation covariances).

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of random vectors to generate.

tools.name: randsample
tools.description: Draw a random sample from a population vector or from the integers 1..n, with or without replacement and with optional selection weights. It is the basis of bootstrap resampling and of random train/test splitting. Setting rng beforehand makes the draw reproducible.
tools.usage:
y = randsample(n, k)
y = randsample(population, k)
y = randsample(___, replace)
y = randsample(___, true, w)

parameters.name: n / population
parameters.description: Upper integer bound or the vector to sample from.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Nonnegative weights proportional to selection probability.

tools.example:
rng(7)
idx = randsample(100, 20);              % 20 without replacement
boot = randsample(1:100, 100, true);    % bootstrap resample
weighted = randsample({'a','b','c'}, 10, true, [0.6 0.3 0.1]);

tools.name: normcdf
tools.description: Evaluate the normal cumulative distribution function, optionally returning confidence bounds when parameter estimates and their covariance are supplied. The 'upper' option computes the right tail accurately even for extreme values. Use it for z-test p-values and normal probability calculations.
tools.usage:
p = normcdf(x)
p = normcdf(x, mu, sigma)
[p, pLo, pUp] = normcdf(x, mu, sigma, pCov, alpha)
p = normcdf(___, 'upper')

parameters.name: pCov, alpha
parameters.description: Parameter covariance and significance level for confidence bounds.

tools.name: norminv
tools.description: Compute the inverse of the normal cumulative distribution function, i.e. the z-value (or x-value) corresponding to a given probability. It is how you obtain critical values for confidence intervals and control limits. Confidence bounds on the quantile can be returned when parameter uncertainty is supplied.
tools.usage:
x = norminv(p)
x = norminv(p, mu, sigma)
[x, xLo, xUp] = norminv(p, mu, sigma, pCov, alpha)
tools.example:
z95 = norminv(0.975)          % 1.9600
limits = norminv([0.001 0.999], 100, 15)
% Three-sigma control limits
ucl = norminv(0.99865, 50, 2);

tools.name: ecdf
tools.description: Compute the empirical cumulative distribution function (Kaplan-Meier estimate) of a sample, with support for right-censored and left-censored data. It also returns pointwise confidence bounds. Call it with no outputs to plot the step function directly.
tools.usage:
[f, x] = ecdf(y)
[f, x, flo, fup] = ecdf(y)
[___] = ecdf(y, Name, Value)
ecdf(y)

parameters.name: 'Frequency'
parameters.description: Counts of observations at each y value.

parameters.name: 'Alpha'
parameters.description: Significance level for the confidence bounds.

tools.name: ksdensity
tools.description: Estimate a probability density (or cdf, survivor, hazard function) nonparametrically by kernel smoothing. The bandwidth controls the smoothness and can be chosen automatically or specified. Support bounds let you avoid leakage past physical limits such as zero.
tools.usage:
[f, xi] = ksdensity(x)
[f, xi, bw] = ksdensity(x, pts)
[___] = ksdensity(___, Name, Value)
ksdensity(x)

tools.name: histfit
tools.description: Plot a histogram of the data with a fitted distribution density curve superimposed. Any distribution supported by fitdist can be overlaid, not just the normal. It is the quickest visual check of whether a parametric model describes the data.
tools.usage:
histfit(x)
histfit(x, nbins)
histfit(x, nbins, dist)
h = histfit(___)

parameters.name: nbins
parameters.description: Number of histogram bins; defaults to the square root of the sample size.

tools.example:
load carsmall
figure
histfit(MPG, 10, 'kernel')
title('MPG with kernel density fit')

tools.name: probplot
tools.description: Create a probability plot comparing sample data against a theoretical distribution, with the axis scaled so a good fit is a straight line. Supports normal, Weibull, lognormal, exponential and other distributions, and can add a reference line from a fitted distribution object. Use it as a visual goodness-of-fit diagnostic.
tools.usage:
probplot(y)
probplot(distname, y)
probplot(ax, pd)
h = probplot(___)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Sample data vector or matrix (columns plotted separately).

parameters.name: pd
parameters.description: A fitted distribution object to add as a reference line.

tools.example:
rng(2)
x = wblrnd(3, 2, 200, 1);
figure, probplot('weibull', x)
figure, probplot('normal', x)   % clearly curved

tools.name: qqplot
tools.description: Produce a quantile-quantile plot of sample quantiles against theoretical (normal by default) quantiles, or against the quantiles of a second sample. Deviations from the straight reference line reveal skewness, heavy tails and outliers. It is the standard normality diagnostic for regression residuals.
tools.usage:
qqplot(x)
qqplot(x, y)
qqplot(x, pd)
qqplot(___, pvec)
h = qqplot(___)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Second sample for a two-sample Q-Q plot.

parameters.name: pd
parameters.description: Probability distribution object to compare against.

tools.name: boxplot
tools.description: Draw box-and-whisker plots showing median, quartiles, whiskers and outliers, optionally grouped by one or more categorical variables. It is the standard way to compare distributions across groups at a glance. Notches give an approximate visual test of median differences.
tools.usage:
boxplot(x)
boxplot(x, g)
boxplot(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: g
parameters.description: Grouping variable (vector, cell array or categorical), or a cell of several for nested grouping.

parameters.name: 'Notch'
parameters.description: 'on' to draw notches indicating median confidence intervals.

tools.example:
load carsmall
boxplot(MPG, Origin, 'Notch', 'on', 'Whisker', 1.5)
ylabel('Miles per gallon')
tools.notes: boxchart is the newer graphics-object-based alternative in base MATLAB.

tools.name: prctile
tools.description: Compute percentiles of a data sample using linear interpolation between order statistics. Accepts a vector of percentages and an optional dimension or 'all' flag. Use it for robust summaries, for clipping outliers and for building empirical confidence intervals.
tools.usage:
Y = prctile(X, p)
Y = prctile(X, p, dim)
Y = prctile(X, p, 'all')
Y = prctile(___, 'Method', method)
tools.notes: quantile(x, p) is the same computation with p expressed as a fraction in [0, 1].

tools.name: quantile
tools.description: Compute sample quantiles for probabilities given as fractions between 0 and 1. It is identical to prctile apart from the scaling of the probability argument. Use it when your thresholds are naturally expressed as probabilities.
tools.usage:
Y = quantile(X, p)
Y = quantile(X, N)
Y = quantile(X, p, dim)
Y = quantile(___, 'Method', method)

parameters.name: N
parameters.description: Integer N returns N equally spaced quantiles.

tools.name: zscore
tools.description: Standardize data to zero mean and unit standard deviation, returning the means and standard deviations used so the same transformation can be applied to new data. Standardization is required by distance-based methods such as k-means, kNN and PCA when variables have different units. Operates column-wise by default.
tools.usage:
Z = zscore(X)
[Z, mu, sigma] = zscore(X)
Z = zscore(X, flag, dim)

parameters.name: flag
parameters.description: 0 (default) for the sample standard deviation (n-1), 1 for the population version (n).

tools.name: normalize
tools.description: Rescale or centre data with a wide choice of methods: z-score, range scaling, median/MAD robust scaling, norm scaling or centring only. It can return the centring and scaling parameters so the same transform can be reapplied to test data. Works on arrays, tables and timetables with variable selection.
tools.usage:
N = normalize(A)
N = normalize(A, method)
N = normalize(A, method, methodtype)
[N, C, S] = normalize(___)
N = normalize(A, 'center', C, 'scale', S)

parameters.name: methodtype
parameters.description: e.g. 'robust' for zscore, [min max] for range, 'median' for center.

tools.name: ttest
tools.description: One-sample or paired-sample t-test of the null hypothesis that data comes from a normal distribution with a specified mean. Returns the test decision, p-value, confidence interval and a statistics structure with the t-statistic and degrees of freedom. Use the two-argument form with two vectors for a paired test.
tools.usage:
h = ttest(x)
h = ttest(x, y)
h = ttest(x, m)
[h, p, ci, stats] = ttest(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Paired observations; the test is applied to x - y.

tools.name: ttest2
tools.description: Two-sample t-test for equal means of two independent samples, assuming normal data. The 'Vartype' option switches between the pooled-variance test and Welch's unequal-variance test, which is safer when group variances differ. Returns the decision, p-value, confidence interval on the mean difference and the test statistics.
tools.usage:
h = ttest2(x, y)
[h, p, ci, stats] = ttest2(x, y, Name, Value)
tools.notes: Check equality of variances first with vartest2, or just use 'unequal' by default.

tools.name: vartest2
tools.description: Two-sample F-test for equal variances of two independent normal samples. Use it to decide whether the pooled-variance form of ttest2 is appropriate. It is quite sensitive to departures from normality, so interpret cautiously.
tools.usage:
h = vartest2(x, y)
[h, p, ci, stats] = vartest2(x, y, Name, Value)
tools.notes: vartestn tests equality of variance across several groups and offers robust Levene and Brown-Forsythe options.

tools.name: anova1
tools.description: One-way analysis of variance testing whether several group means are all equal. It returns the p-value, an ANOVA table and a stats structure needed for post-hoc comparisons, and by default displays the table and a boxplot. Use multcompare on the stats output to find which specific groups differ.
tools.usage:
p = anova1(y)
p = anova1(y, group)
[p, tbl, stats] = anova1(y, group, displayopt)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Matrix (columns are groups) or vector of responses.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: Grouping variable when y is a vector.

parameters.name: displayopt
parameters.description: 'on' (default) or 'off' to suppress the table and plot.

tools.name: anovan
tools.description: N-way analysis of variance for designs with several crossed or nested grouping factors, including interaction terms, random effects and continuous covariates. It handles unbalanced designs with a choice of sums-of-squares type. Use it whenever more than one factor may influence the response.
tools.usage:
p = anovan(y, group)
[p, tbl, stats, terms] = anovan(y, group, Name, Value)

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: Cell array of grouping variables, one per factor.

parameters.name: 'varnames'
parameters.description: Names of the factors for the output table.

parameters.name: 'random'
parameters.description: Indices of factors to treat as random effects.

parameters.name: 'continuous'
parameters.description: Indices of factors that are continuous covariates.

tools.name: multcompare
tools.description: Perform post-hoc multiple comparisons of group means (or other estimated marginal means) with control of the family-wise error rate. It returns a matrix of pairwise differences with confidence intervals and p-values, and draws an interactive comparison plot. Use it after anova1, anovan, kruskalwallis or a fitted model.
tools.usage:
c = multcompare(stats)
[c, m, h, gnames] = multcompare(stats, Name, Value)
results = multcompare(mdl)

parameters.name: stats
parameters.description: Statistics structure from anova1, anovan, kruskalwallis, friedman, etc.

parameters.name: 'Dimension'
parameters.description: Which factors to compare for anovan results.

tools.name: kruskalwallis
tools.description: Nonparametric one-way ANOVA on ranks, testing whether samples from several groups come from the same distribution. It makes no normality assumption, which makes it the natural fallback when anova1's assumptions fail. Its stats output can be passed to multcompare.
tools.usage:
p = kruskalwallis(x)
p = kruskalwallis(x, group)
[p, tbl, stats] = kruskalwallis(x, group, displayopt)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Matrix (columns are groups) or vector of data.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: Grouping variable for a vector x.

tools.name: ranksum
tools.description: Wilcoxon rank sum test (equivalent to the Mann-Whitney U test) for equal medians of two independent samples. It is the nonparametric counterpart of ttest2 and is robust to outliers and non-normality. For small samples it computes an exact p-value.
tools.usage:
p = ranksum(x, y)
[p, h, stats] = ranksum(x, y, Name, Value)

tools.name: signrank
tools.description: Wilcoxon signed rank test for a one-sample or paired-sample median, the nonparametric analogue of ttest. It assumes only that the differences are symmetric about the median, not that they are normal. Exact p-values are computed for small samples.
tools.usage:
p = signrank(x)
p = signrank(x, y)
p = signrank(x, m)
[p, h, stats] = signrank(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Paired sample; the test is applied to x - y.

tools.name: kstest
tools.description: One-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit test comparing the empirical CDF of the data with a specified continuous distribution (standard normal by default). It returns the test decision, p-value and the maximum CDF discrepancy. Note that estimating the distribution's parameters from the same data invalidates the p-value.
tools.usage:
h = kstest(x)
h = kstest(x, Name, Value)
[h, p, ksstat, cv] = kstest(___)

parameters.name: 'CDF'
parameters.description: A two-column [x F(x)] matrix or a distribution object giving the hypothesized CDF.

tools.notes: Use lillietest when the normal parameters are estimated from the data.

tools.name: kstest2
tools.description: Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the null hypothesis that two samples come from the same continuous distribution. It requires no assumption about the distributional family and is sensitive to differences in location, scale and shape. The samples may have different lengths.
tools.usage:
h = kstest2(x1, x2)
[h, p, ks2stat] = kstest2(x1, x2, Name, Value)

tools.name: lillietest
tools.description: Lilliefors test for normality (or exponentiality/extreme value) when the distribution parameters are estimated from the data. This corrects the bias that makes a plain kstest too conservative in that situation. It is the appropriate default normality test for regression residuals.
tools.usage:
h = lillietest(x)
[h, p, kstat, critval] = lillietest(x, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'MCTol'
parameters.description: Monte Carlo tolerance for computing p-values outside the tabulated range.

tools.name: jbtest
tools.description: Jarque-Bera test of normality based on the sample skewness and kurtosis. It is powerful against distributions with the wrong tail behaviour and is a standard diagnostic on regression and econometric residuals. Use the Monte Carlo option for small samples where the asymptotic chi-square approximation is poor.
tools.usage:
h = jbtest(x)
[h, p, jbstat, critval] = jbtest(x, alpha, mctol)

parameters.name: mctol
parameters.description: Monte Carlo standard error tolerance for the p-value.

tools.name: adtest
tools.description: Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit test, which weights the tails of the distribution more heavily than the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. It can test against a fully specified distribution or one whose parameters are estimated from the data. Often the most powerful of the common normality tests.
tools.usage:
h = adtest(x)
[h, p, adstat, cv] = adtest(x, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'MCTol'
parameters.description: Monte Carlo tolerance for p-value computation.

tools.name: chi2gof
tools.description: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test comparing binned observed frequencies with those expected under a hypothesized distribution. It works for discrete as well as continuous distributions and automatically pools bins with small expected counts. Degrees of freedom are reduced for each parameter estimated from the data.
tools.usage:
h = chi2gof(x)
[h, p, stats] = chi2gof(x, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'CDF'
parameters.description: Distribution object or function handle giving the hypothesized CDF.

parameters.name: 'Expected'
parameters.description: Expected counts per bin, as an alternative to a CDF.

parameters.name: 'EMin'
parameters.description: Minimum expected count per bin before pooling (default 5).

parameters.name: 'NParams'
parameters.description: Number of parameters estimated from the data.

tools.name: corr
tools.description: Compute pairwise linear (Pearson), rank (Spearman) or concordance (Kendall) correlation coefficients between the columns of one or two matrices, together with p-values for testing zero correlation. Missing data can be handled pairwise or by complete rows. Use Spearman or Kendall when the relationship is monotone but not linear.
tools.usage:
rho = corr(X)
rho = corr(X, Y)
[rho, pval] = corr(___, Name, Value)

tools.name: partialcorr
tools.description: Compute partial correlation coefficients between variables while controlling for the linear effect of a set of covariates. This reveals direct relationships that a simple correlation may attribute to a shared confounder. Returns p-values along with the coefficients.
tools.usage:
rho = partialcorr(X)
rho = partialcorr(X, Z)
rho = partialcorr(X, Y, Z)
[rho, pval] = partialcorr(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: X, Y
parameters.description: Data matrices whose columns are correlated.

parameters.name: Z
parameters.description: Matrix of covariates to control for.
